entries.title: My Year in Paris With Gertrude Stein by Deborah Levy audiobook review – gripping vision of a fearless writer
entries.summary: A fictional British author in Paris sets out to explore Stein through the lens of her own friendships, in this inventive, perfectly paced portraitIt is late 2024, and an unnamed British author living in Paris is trying to write an essay on Gertrude Stein, the modernist writer and art collector. The author has been distracted by her friend Eva’s cat, who is lost and whose name is “it” in lower case
entries.content:
It is late 2024, and an unnamed British author living in Paris is trying to write an essay on Gertrude Stein, the modernist writer and art collector. The author has been distracted by her friend Eva’s cat, who is lost and whose name is “it” in lower case, which inevitably leads to confusion – has Eva lost her cat or her mind? (Her other friend, Fanny, has rechristened the cat Bob, to make talking about him easier.)

The Pennsylvania-born Stein was painted by Picasso, hung out with Hemingway and wrote strange, stream-of-consciousness prose long before James Joyce embarked on his masterwork Ulysses. Commercial success didn’t come until she was in her 60s with The Autobiography of Alice B Toklas, a biography of her partner and one of her more accessible books. Our narrator is an admirer of Stein’s work, yet she can be exasperated by it. “Sometimes, when I read her baffling and beguiling writing I want to smack it in the chops. [Stein] longed for her readers to find her, yet there was a part of her that could not bear to be found.”

A blend of fiction and biography, Deborah Levy’s ninth novel is read by voice actor Kristin Atherton; her narration is cool, precise and perfectly paced. We follow the author as she goes to Père Lachaise cemetery in search of Stein’s grave and where she reflects on the lives of other literary luminaries, and on her own friendships. The Stein who emerges in this unusual and gripping portrait is fearless, innovative and, the author notes, “so forward-looking that she never learned to reverse her Ford Model T”.

Available via Penguin, 3hr 54min

Further listening

Nonesuch

Francis Spufford, Faber, 15hr 29min

Set during the blitz, this genre-bending thriller finds Iris Hawkins, a smart young office clerk, navigating a chance encounter which propels her into a world of necromancy, time-travelling Nazis and a plot to assassinate Winston Churchill.

The Delusions

Jenni Fagan, Penguin, 8hr 19min

Fagan’s satirical novel about the afterlife centres on Edi, who works in “the largest soul terminus in existence” where she processes the newly dead and decides where they should go based on how they lived their lives. Read by the author.

entries.title: Margaret Busby: ‘My friend Bonnie Greer fearlessly spoke out and forged connections’
entries.summary: The writer and editor shares memories of a creative powerhouse who was generous with her time and expertiseBonnie Greer, writer and cultural commentator, dies aged 77Bonnie Greer personified courage, humour, principle and generosity. Before knowing her in person, I met her work. Her 1994 debut novel Hanging by Her Teeth – about a Black American woman travelling through the US and Europe in search
entries.content:
Bonnie Greer personified courage, humour, principle and generosity. Before knowing her in person, I met her work. Her 1994 debut novel Hanging by Her Teeth – about a Black American woman travelling through the US and Europe in search of her father – was sent to me for endorsement by its publisher, and I commented unhesitatingly: “Writing with sharpness, wit and poignancy, Bonnie Greer gathers the sequestered memories behind one Black woman’s bitter-sweet blues.”

The scope of Bonnie’s own life is beyond anything fictional, encompassing highs and lows, triumphs and challenges, her trajectory starting in the West Side of Chicago and ending up navigating iconic areas of London – whether Holland Park or Covent Garden or Soho – as if to the manor born. It was an honour to become her friend, sharing many a good time, offering a consoling shoulder if needed. An added bonus was to meet her husband David Hutchins. What a wonderful mutually supportive team they made.

Bonnie’s activism marched side by side with her creativity and powers of persuasion. Friendship, support, empathy and behind-the-scenes involvement were all part of who she was. She could be effervescently sociable. There was an era when she relished get-togethers of a sort of ladies-who-lunch club that she would organise, where we might chat for hours, exchanging memories, planning dreamy never-to-be-fulfilled projects. I recall one gathering that took place at the House of Commons – with Diane Abbott, Verna Wilkins, Maya Jaggi and Nana Ayebia Clarke – when Bonnie suddenly made us all pause to reflect on the fact we were all sitting there, with a view of the Thames and London’s landscape, given where we had come from.

Seemingly ready to re-invent herself, she was perhaps defying anyone to easily label her. She could be public intellectual, television pundit, dramatist, librettist, academic. Her repertoire was wide-ranging and ever-expanding, with fresh ideas emerging at every opportunity. She fearlessly spoke out, forged new connections, took on weighty burdens.

She lent expertise to numerous national cultural institutions – including on the boards of the British Museum, the Royal Opera House and the London Film School, and as vice president of the Shaw Society and chancellor of Kingston University London. She shared her vision with such ventures as the Black Theatre Co-operative and Talawa Theatre Company (where, during her stint as artistic director, she mooted an ambitious dramatisation of my 1,000-plus-page anthology, Daughters of Africa). We were both patrons of the SI Leeds Literary Prize for unpublished fiction by Black and Asian women in the UK.

It was pure delight to accompany her anywhere to experience music, art, drama, film or anything intellectually stimulating.

In June 2019, we went to a lecture by Lonnie Bunch III at the British Library – then newly appointed to secretary of the Smithsonian Institution, the first African American and first historian appointed to do so, who recently announced his intention to retire at the end of 2026. Dr Bunch’s recent communication with me echoes my own feelings: “I have been made better by my interactions with Bonnie. She was generous with her time, with her contacts and with her friendship. Her passing is an immeasurable loss. I am crying but also smiling because of her impact on so many. She was simply amazing. Her ability to speak truth to power made her such a unique voice in both the UK and the US.”

We will all miss her.

entries.title: The Strangers by Naomi Alderman review – where has this odd new species come from?
entries.summary: A bereavement memoir mingles with speculative fiction, in a wise and ragged examination of grief from the author of The PowerIn his Remarks on Frazer’s Golden Bough, Ludwig Wittgenstein alludes to an incident that followed the death of Franz Schubert. He recalls that Schubert’s brother cut several scores into small pieces, each consisting of only a few bars of music, and handed them out to Schuber
entries.content:
In his Remarks on Frazer’s Golden Bough, Ludwig Wittgenstein alludes to an incident that followed the death of Franz Schubert. He recalls that Schubert’s brother cut several scores into small pieces, each consisting of only a few bars of music, and handed them out to Schubert’s favourite pupils. This, Wittgenstein argues, was a totally understandable act of grief. He goes on to suggest, however, that if, in his grief, Schubert’s brother had left the scores untouched, or even burned them, then that too would be equally legible to us. Such is the disorienting nature of loss – in its wake, anything goes.

In The Strangers, Women’s prize-winning author Naomi Alderman tests this thesis to its limits. How about dealing with grief by writing an uneasy memoir/speculative fiction hybrid about the sudden appearance of a new species of quasi-badgers that seem to improve the quality of local soil?

Well, it turns out Wittgenstein was right. The Strangers, despite (or perhaps because of) its many ragged idiosyncrasies, is a remarkably successful evocation of loss. Narrated by “the novelist Naomi Alderman”, who is mourning both her recently deceased mother and a series of failed pregnancies, the book ranges incisively across the vast affective terrain bequeathed to those who go on living: despair, disorientation, solipsism, petulance, regret, resignation … the list goes on. After all, grief is not an emotion – it is all the emotions, all at once.

And by braiding the memoir within a subtly unnerving tale of eco-horror infestation, Alderman substantially raises the philosophical and symbolic stakes. It is a high-risk, sporadically successful manoeuvre, but one that recognises the gravity of the task at hand. In the same way that a gravestone is an attempt to give form to an absence, Alderman’s structural ingenuity allows the reader to wrangle some of the ineffable aspects of grief into something more coherent and bounded.

The plot itself is simple enough, and relatively small fry compared to some of Alderman’s previous work, such as thwarting the techno-apocalypse (The Future) or upending the global gender hierarchy (The Power). A new type of species is discovered, a flat-faced and long-nosed mammal that comes to be known as a mimmoth. They remain largely inscrutable to humans: hard to photograph, even harder to capture, and seemingly responsible for a range of positive ecological changes. Their inscrutability cuts both ways, however, and soon enough the mimmoths are the subject of conspiracy theories and hate campaigns, worship and veneration, floating signifiers swept up into the insatiable polarisation of the present. To some they are harbingers of a better future, sent to teach us how to care for one another and the planet, while to others they are “invaders, genetic freaks, not natural”.

On the whole, Alderman handles the fairly obvious political allegories with a lightness of touch that prevents them from collapsing into polemic, sketching out our political and media environment with the skill of a practised world-builder. The failing institutions of British life are a “Potemkin village” stripped of their engine and replaced with “a clockwork mechanism, slowly running down”. There are occasional moments, however, that seem transplanted from another era entirely; one when people’s political subjectivities were formed by front pages and evening news bulletins, and not by unchecked genocide livestreamed to their phones.

Fundamentally, though, The Strangers is a deeply moving and wise book, asserting the painful truth that we simply do not get to choose the things that we lose. When the narrator wonders if she has fallen prey to “mimmoth-psychosis”, the delusion that one has a uniquely intimate relation with the mysterious creatures, I was put in mind of Judith Butler’s observation about grief being a site of temporal reorganisation, a crucible in which our selfhood can be undone and remade. Both Alderman and Butler seem to remind us that while despair may temporarily convince us otherwise, life, in all its terrifying potential, stubbornly persists.

That the mimmoths’ arrival coincides with an upsurge in mushroom-like fungus seems particularly telling. Among its many miraculous properties, mycelium contains within it a biological code of deep sociality and connectivity, existing as a network that is constantly reallocating and rebalancing resources, moving nutrients symbiotically between the old and the young, the weak and the strong. The political metaphor contained therein has proved irresistible to many commentators. But in The Strangers, Alderman asks whether there is also a parallel to be drawn in how we allocate our resources of attention and love more proximately. How do we mediate between the existing potential of our own lives, the expired potential of the dead and the unrealised potential of the never or nearly born? It is the type of intractable question one can only ever hope to live alongside. Or, as “the novelist Naomi Alderman” puts it, “I do not wish my ghosts away.”

entries.title: The New Dark Ages by James Marriott review – a grandiose but superficial defence of reading
entries.summary: What is it that makes books so magical? The Times columnist somehow forgets to tell us in this lofty polemicWhile other kids watched cartoons, Times columnist James Marriott would spend his school holidays in bed with piles of books – “a mammoth effort of attention, perhaps the greatest I ever made” – under the spell of his father, a teacher who inculcated in him a literary zeal “not exactly commo
entries.content:
While other kids watched cartoons, Times columnist James Marriott would spend his school holidays in bed with piles of books – “a mammoth effort of attention, perhaps the greatest I ever made” – under the spell of his father, a teacher who inculcated in him a literary zeal “not exactly common in the north of England in the early 2000s”.

Twenty-five years on, Marriott fears smartphones have all but killed reading for everyone. He had to get rid of his own – “George Eliot is no match” – and now, watching the rest of us scroll, he worries not only that we will lose the ability to appreciate Middlemarch, but that we risk falling prey to tyrants and anti-vaxxers forging “a world very different to the one we have known … mystical, tribal and autocratic”.

Such is the gist of Marriott’s first book, The New Dark Ages, a polemical elegy tracing the rise and fall of print from Montaigne to Mr Beast. The point is modest – scroll less, read more – but the tone is grandiose. Literacy turbocharged our capacity for complex argument, he argues, but adds that “conversation is very far from useless”, and says “literate civilisation … has never produced a work of art with quite the same quality of heroic starkness as the Iliad or Beowulf”.

The readerly bicep Marriott likes flashing is rarely as firm as it looks. “The important things Leo Tolstoy [has] to say about life will only be understood if you can pay attention,” he writes, never saying what they are. His advocacy for books relies on browbeating hyperbole: “I believe there is a kind of truth about life which is only accessible through prose fiction with its capacity to show us the inside of other minds … It is the reason that no actor on earth can show with his or her face what Jane Austen can show us about the human heart in half a paragraph.” When he actually articulates a novel’s impact, it’s to tell us that Elena Ferrante taught him “what it is like to be a teenage girl”.

Literature isn’t his only focus. “In the early 20th century everyone read a newspaper,” he says, lamenting social media’s impact on politics. He imagines a print report and a TikTok clip from the same war zone: “Even the most simple written article is more likely to offer explanations for events. How did the war start? Why did the war start?” Alternatively, to summon “your rage with an image, I only need to show you a picture of … heaped bodies”; in other words, if you’re angry when “a missile destroys an apartment block in the Middle East” – the clip he envisages – it’s because a journalist hasn’t explained it.

The sense grows that lofty proclamations and punchy quips aren’t enough to keep the book afloat in deep waters. “The 21st century’s much-documented epidemic of anxiety, depression and purposelessness is at least partly rooted in the … culture of the screen,” says Marriott, leaving us to wonder if he’s muddled symptom and cause. When the book begins, he calls smartphones the “major culprit” of the drop in reading for pleasure – “factors like inequality” are less to blame – but it ends by warning that “very rich” people have the resources “to keep their children away from addictive screens. Poorer parents who have to work multiple jobs and who lack the money for childcare do not.”

It’s the last gasp for a thesis whose apocalyptic urgency fizzles out in equivocating caveats. “Post-literate”, Marriott clarifies, doesn’t mean “incapable of reading and writing”: although there may be “fewer Shakespeares, more Slack messages” – how many Shakespeares does he think there have been? – literacy “still has a future”. Which isn’t “to counsel unthinking optimism”, just to say that “even in the worst-case scenario, reading … will be around for a while yet”. Phew!

The New Dark Ages is neatly positioned to appeal to lapsed readers who wince at their weekly screen time report. But there’s a less opportunistic book buried deep between its lines: one about growing up convinced the world begins and ends with literature, only to find that all it took to make you doubt it was a six-inch sliver of black glass.

entries.title: Singapore pays people to pick up a book in battle against doomscrolling
entries.summary: Affluent city-state hopes plan will improve critical thinking and imagination ‘in a world of extraordinary abundance of stimulation’Singapore is paying its citizens to pick up a book for at least 15 minutes a day in an effort to fight the rise of doomscrolling.The affluent city-state hopes its gamification strategy, which launched this month, will improve concentration, critical thinking and the i
entries.content:
Singapore is paying its citizens to pick up a book for at least 15 minutes a day in an effort to fight the rise of doomscrolling.

The affluent city-state hopes its gamification strategy, which launched this month, will improve concentration, critical thinking and the imagination of Singaporeans.

Under the scheme, readers accrue points that can be redeemed for a few cents. People will have to log 50 daily reading sessions on a government website to earn S$1 (80c). A session of 15 minutes or more is rewarded with 20 virtual coins, with 1,000 coins needed for a dollar payment. One reading session is allowed daily.

The national library board’s chief, Melissa Tam, said sustainable reading habits were built through small and achievable steps.

“We live in a world of extraordinary abundance, of content, information and stimulation,” she told the Straits Times. “At any moment, we can scroll through hundreds of headlines, watch a video or get a summary of almost anything.

“We know that habits are built through small, consistent actions. So, we are starting with a simple goal: just read for 15 minutes a day. On the bus, before bed or over lunch.”

The government is considering ways to make social media less harmful for young Singaporeans, including a daily time limit. Doomscrolling and addiction caused most harm to young people, a recent study found.

It is not uncommon for the Singapore government to use financial incentives to try to influence the behaviour of its citizens. Previous health-focused initiatives have included supermarket vouchers for walking and prizes for hitting daily step targets.

Despite government concerns about reading, Singapore’s 15-year-old students recently topped the world rankings for reading in the 2025 Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), beating China and Taiwan.

entries.title: Redwood by Ben Macintyre review – a superbly wrought tale of cold war defection
entries.summary: This story of Soviet agent and his MI6 handler in revolutionary Iran is a page-turning masterpieceBen Macintyre uses the acronym MICE to describe the reasons people betray their countries: Money, Ideology, Coercion or Ego. In the set-piece that opens his latest work of true-espionage, we discover a new reason: erectile dysfunction.Stressed, drinking too much, under constant surveillance, furious a
entries.content:
Ben Macintyre uses the acronym MICE to describe the reasons people betray their countries: Money, Ideology, Coercion or Ego. In the set-piece that opens his latest work of true-espionage, we discover a new reason: erectile dysfunction.

Stressed, drinking too much, under constant surveillance, furious about the corruption of his colleagues and frustrated with his home life, the KGB’s Vladimir Kuzichkin is offering to betray the secrets of his homeland and its Iranian allies, if only a British doctor can help him have sex again.

If you have read Macintyre before, you’ll recognise a classic example of his style: the journalist’s eye for salacious detail combined with a historian’s rigour. The rest of Redwood lives up to the attention-grabbing opening scene; I devoured it in a single sitting.

If you haven’t read him, he is the author of a hatful of bestselling books about war, politics and secrecy, several of which have been adapted for the screen, and one of which – Operation Mincemeat – has become a West End and Broadway musical. They are sometimes derided as “dadlit”, the kind of nonfiction read by golf club bores and armchair colonels. But Redwood is as far above yet-another-book-about-the-second-world-war as a George Smiley novel is above Jack Reacher.

The setting is the immediate aftermath of the 1979 revolution that brought Iran’s ayatollahs to power. The west was on the back foot, having lost a key ally, with the Americans particularly discomfited by Islamists having seized their embassy and taken its staff hostage. The Soviets, meanwhile, thought they had an opportunity to spread their influence south, to a strategic and oil-rich country with warm water ports.

Kuzichkin’s job was to further this aim by distributing money, arms and encouragement to the Tudeh party, an orthodox communist movement led by a Stalinist who had spent the previous few decades in exile in East Germany. He ran his operation out of the huge Soviet embassy, where his mostly useless colleagues celebrated even the smallest of successes with vast quantities of vodka, and he really hated it.

Literally across the street, in the equally large British embassy, was Ian McCredie, a young MI6 operative who had recently arrived in Tehran with a wife and baby in tow, his task to re-establish a British intelligence presence after the entire team had been forced to leave. He didn’t drink as much as Kuzichkin, but he did discover 50 crates of whisky that a predecessor had imported as a present for the Shah and left in a garage, so was able to ride out the revolutionaries’ ban on alcohol quite well.

The relationship between the two men, which becomes one of handler and double agent, is the backbone of the book. It is set against the ever-present risk of discovery by the Revolutionary Guard, and given added poignancy by the fact that neither one realises their actions are taking place amid a geopolitical tectonic shift, in which the communists are slipping into irrelevance and the Islamists rising to take their place.

This is demonstrated most starkly when, after Kuzichkin has been safely exfiltrated to the UK for debriefing, his controllers send him to Pakistan to share his intelligence about the communists with the Iranian authorities. They hoped this would win them favour in Tehran, but instead it unleashes an orgy of violence and torture against Tudeh supporters which further entrenches the Islamic Republic’s control and does nothing to help the west.

But such weighty matters are leavened throughout by witty turns of phrase: an antiquated coding machine is “not so much user-unfriendly, as overtly hostile”; the head of Britain’s mission in Tehran is “a master of the art of thinking twice before saying nothing”; McCredie’s wife Lucy had nothing to fear from living under an oppressive regime because “she had been educated in an English girls’ boarding school”. So, by all means give Redwood to your father for Christmas, but make sure you read it yourself first: it’s superb.

entries.title: Safe Spaces by Tice Cin review – a kaleidoscopic vision of precarity, music and grief
entries.summary: Part spoken-word poem, part journalistic meditation, this is an inventive, tender novel of a songwriter’s journey through love and loss in LondonTice Cin’s philosophical and poetic new novel about a young Turkish-Cypriot songwriter and music producer extends the preoccupations of her prizewinning debut, 2021’s Keeping the House. This intimately told sophomore novel, again a story of friendship, pr
entries.content:
Tice Cin’s philosophical and poetic new novel about a young Turkish-Cypriot songwriter and music producer extends the preoccupations of her prizewinning debut, 2021’s Keeping the House. This intimately told sophomore novel, again a story of friendship, precarity and community, is at once an elegy, a spoken-word poem and a journalistic meditation, repeatedly asking readers: “So, are you listening?”

For our unnamed narrator, “hurts come in different shapes each time”: from the childhood scars of her father’s abandonment, to sexism in the creative scene and the difficulties of navigating short-lived flatshares on universal credit (“If you don’t know about being money dry, if you don’t know loss – you don’t get it. If you know, you know”). Her journey of personal discovery is mapped on to the contemporary travails of London’s wider working-class inner-city diaspora communities as she calculates her life by doorways, “walking past each one” without a roadmap for her personal and professional goals.

At the centre of the novel is the loss of the narrator’s closest confidante, referred to as “My Favourite Person”. As his untimely death becomes fodder for gossip, she addresses those questioning how he died: “You’re asking for information but to me it’s the loop, the scaffolding, never comes down, this con of process, all dying to know how he died.” Meanwhile, she remembers their late-night phone calls, continues to leave him unheard voicemails: “Don’t want to do it all without you on my team.”

How to survive in a world darkened by an unshakeable loss? “Memories are a bit like a messy laundry cupboard. Whenever you brush past the door, all the items inside are falling out… Jamming the door doesn’t help because everything is still messy inside.” Through love affairs and short-term jobs, in DJ booths or on dancefloors of local raves, in therapy sessions and beauty parlours, the grieving narrator attempts to articulate herself creatively and emotionally. “Sometimes my head feels like the city, ambulances going past 24/7 but we still hear nothing. In a way it’s a type of growth, to feel the wrong things less.”

In Cin’s dexterous hands, form meets content to kaleidoscopic effect. Told in the first person and without character names, most vignettes are additionally prefaced with a clarification of who is being addressed, or doing the addressing: “The ‘you’ is reading me. The ‘me’ is still me.” “The ‘she’ is all of us, me.” “I am ‘her’ and ‘you’.” With a protagonist deep in the world of music, these shape-shifting perspectives give the impression of a DJ spinning tracks.

In the narrator’s own safe space, she is “a marshmallow gravity genie who sleeps facefront on a soft cloud”, floating away from earthly human concerns. This is a tender novel looking for a foothold in an alienating world.
